intro: Check what really supports a survey and whether the headline promises more than the data allows us to claim.
b1.titulo: What the data says and what the headline adds
b1.texto:
A data point and a headline do not say the same thing, even when they use the same words. The data is what was measured; the headline is an interpretation.

Before taking something as certain, ask yourself three things:

1. **Who was asked?** If the survey was voluntary and online, the people who answered were the ones who wanted to.
2. **How many answered?** One hundred and twenty-eight out of two hundred and forty is not “most of the population”.
3. **What can be concluded?** From a sample like that you can say “some”, not “almost all”.

The headline that jumps from the sample to the population makes a leap that the data does not authorise.
b2.f0.texto: The headline says that almost everyone uses the bike.
b2.f1.texto: The survey, however, was voluntary and online.
b2.f2.texto: The sample, then, is not representative.
b2.f3.texto: The headline promises more than the data allows.
b4.texto:
Data is presented with graded expressions. These are not the same:

- **casi todos** (more than ninety per cent)
- **la mayoría** (more than half)
- **muchos** (a significant part, with no figure)
- **algunos** (a minority)

And there are verbs that mark the strength of the conclusion: **sugerir** is weak, **indicar** is medium, **demostrar** is strong. A headline usually goes up a level: what the report presents as a suggestion, the headline presents as proof.

Watch out also for **representativo**: a sample is representative if it was chosen at random and reflects the group. If the people who chose to take part were the ones who picked it, it is not.
b4.e0.texto: One hundred and twenty-eight people said they used the bike.
b4.e1.texto: The sample does not allow us to conclude that it is a general habit.
b5.f0.texto: An online survey received two hundred and forty voluntary responses.
b5.f1.texto: One hundred and twenty-eight people said they used the bicycle at least once a week.
b5.f2.texto: The newspaper's headline summed up the result in a single sentence.
b5.f3.texto: The sample does not allow us to conclude that it is a general habit.
b5.f4.texto: The people who answered were interested in the topic and had internet access.
b5.f5.texto: A headline that promises more than the data supports is a misleading headline.
b6.pregunta: What can be claimed with this survey?
b6.o0: That some of the people who answered use the bike.
b6.o0.refuerzo: Correct: that is the only thing the sample supports without going beyond it.
b6.o1: That most of the population uses the bike.
b6.o1.refuerzo: Incorrect: the sample does not represent the population, so it cannot be generalised.
b6.o2: That nobody uses the bike in that city.
b6.o2.refuerzo: Incorrect: the data says just the opposite.
b7.o0.refuerzo: Correct: it agrees with «muestra», which is feminine.
b7.o1.refuerzo: Incorrect: that is the masculine form.
b9.pregunta: Write in Spanish: «The sample is not representative».
p.el dato.glosa: concrete information that has been measured
p.el dato.consejo: «Dato» is the piece of information; the plural «datos» is the usual form. You «contrastas» a dato, you check it against other sources.
p.la encuesta.glosa: study that asks questions to a group of people
p.la encuesta.consejo: You «realizas» or «llevas a cabo» a survey; you do not «haces» one in a formal text.
p.el porcentaje.glosa: a part out of a hundred
p.el porcentaje.consejo: Mind the pronunciation: por-then-TA-he. The «j» sounds strong.
p.representativo.glosa: that reflects the group studied well
p.representativo.consejo: You say «representativo de», not «representativo a»: «una muestra representativa de la ciudad».
p.concluir.glosa: to reach an idea after analysing the data
p.concluir.consejo: Irregular: concluyo, concluyes. And after «concluir que» the subjunctive is usual if it is a hypothesis.
p.la muestra.glosa: group of people or cases that is studied
p.la muestra.consejo: Not to be confused with «la muestra» of a shop or a trade fair.
p.el titular.glosa: the large sentence a news item starts with
p.el titular.consejo: It also means «persona que tiene un título». The context makes it clear.
p.el sesgo.glosa: an inclination that distorts a result
p.el sesgo.consejo: You say «un sesgo de selección». Verb: sesgar.
p.la evidencia.consejo: In academic Spanish, «evidencia» is required for a strong claim, not an impression.
p.usan.consejo: From «usar», to use. The «-an» ending is for «ellos» or «ellas».
p.voluntaria.consejo: The «v» sounds like «b», and the «ia» is a diphthong. It means done by choice.
p.representativa.consejo: From «representar», to represent. The feminine «-a» agrees with «muestra», which is feminine.
p.veintiocho.consejo: Written as one word in Spanish. The «v» reads «b», and the «ch» is one sound.
p.usaban.consejo: From «usar». The «-aban» ending is the imperfect, used for habits in the past.
p.general.consejo: The «g» before «e» sounds like «h». It means applies to most people, not only a few.
p.recibió.consejo: From «recibir», to receive. The accent on the «ó» marks the past tense for «él».
p.voluntarias.consejo: Feminine plural of «voluntaria». It agrees with «respuestas», which is feminine.
p.resumió.consejo: From «resumir», to summarise. The accent on the «ó» marks the past tense for «él» or «ella».
p.respondió.consejo: From «responder», to answer. The accent on the «ó» marks the past tense.
p.tema.consejo: Though it ends in «-a», «tema» is masculine: «el tema». Remember the article to use it right.
p.acceso.consejo: The «cc» has a hard «k» then a «th» sound: «ak-THE-so». It is what you have to get in.
p.engañoso.consejo: From «engañar», to deceive. The «ñ» is pronounced «ny» and the stress falls on «NYO».
p.algunas.consejo: «Algunas» means some, in the feminine plural. The «gu» before «a» is read «gu».
p.respondieron.consejo: From «responder». The «-ieron» ending is the past for «ellos» or «ustedes».
